outline.text: Where every figure and claim in this run comes from.
One row per traced paragraph, row or figure. Open a row to see how it was derived.
Stable credit with thin headroom: leverage is falling, but the 2028 notes need refinancing.
Input Net debt = gross debt − cash
Excerpt “Adjusted EBITDA for the twelve months ended 30 September 2026 was USD 486 million (2025: USD 441 million).”
Three customers bring 58% of revenue and one engine programme 34%.
Parts and repair bring 44% of revenue and about three fifths of gross profit.
Working capital absorbed USD 71m as inventory was built for the engine ramp.
A first-lien covenant applies only when the facility is more than 40% drawn.
Net leverage above 5.0x at a year end, or no agreed refinancing of the 2028 notes by 30 June 2027, moves the view to negative.
New-build contracts run five to seven years at fixed prices.
Four small purchases since 2023 added product lines.
Two airlines have begun certifying alternative parts; none has passed certification.
One certified alternative on a top-ten part, or a third slip in the engine programme’s ramp, would move the view from stable to weakening.
Engine programme delay: Medium probability, high impact.
Loss of sole-source status: Low probability, high impact.
Customer concentration: Medium probability, medium impact.
Input cost inflation: High probability, low impact.
Tariff exposure: Probability not recorded, medium impact.
Engine deliveries per month: Below 40 for two quarters.
Aftermarket price rise at renewal: Below 3%.
Alternative parts certified: Any top-ten part.
Aftermarket share of gross profit: Below 55%.
Aftermarket pricing is durable for the parts where Halden is the only certified source.
About four fifths of the order book is under firm contracts.
A sole-source aftermarket franchise carries a thinner, more cyclical original-equipment business.
Management says no alternative part has passed certification.
The module gave no source for this claim.
Headroom against covenant and rating triggers
Interest cover against the peer range
Nothing above USD 50m falls due before March 2028, and one springing covenant stands between lenders and a debt-funded purchase.
Baskets allow roughly USD 400m of further secured debt, which the sponsor has used for purchases before.
The security and intercreditor documents were not provided.
Peer figures for two companies are on a reported basis while the issuer is company-adjusted.
Customer names and contract terms come from management presentations, not from contracts.
The share of revenue under cost pass-through clauses is not established for this run.
The hedge schedule was not among the files provided.
The only source for the average cost of debt is marked confidential.
The lease maturity schedule is not in the files, so leases appear in the stack but not by year.
